quick_notes.title: Reporting Verb
quick_notes.detail: If reporting verb is in Past (Said), the tense inside changes. Said -> Said. Said to -> Told. (Exception: Universal Truths/Facts).
quick_notes.explanation: When you are telling someone what another person said, you use a reporting verb like "said" or "told." If that reporting verb is in the past tense, for example "he said," then the verbs inside the quoted part usually change to a more past form; for instance, "I am happy" becomes "he said he was happy." The verb "said" stays as "said" when no person is mentioned after it, but "said to" changes to "told," as in "he said to me" becomes "he told me." The only exception is when the statement is a universal truth or a general fact, like "the sun rises in the east," because the tense inside does not change even if the reporting verb is past.

quick_notes.title: Tense Backshift
quick_notes.detail: Present Simple -> Past Simple. Present Cont -> Past Cont. Present Perfect -> Past Perfect. Past Simple -> Past Perfect.
quick_notes.explanation: Tense backshift is the rule for changing verbs when you report what someone said using a past tense reporting verb like "said" or "told." For example, if the original statement uses the Present Simple tense (which describes habits or facts, like "I walk"), you change it to the Past Simple tense ("I walked"). If the original uses the Present Continuous tense (action happening now, like "I am walking"), you change it to the Past Continuous tense ("I was walking"). If the original uses the Present Perfect tense (action completed recently, like "I have walked"), you change it to the Past Perfect tense ("I had walked"). Finally, if the original uses the Past Simple tense itself ("I walked"), you also change it to the Past Perfect tense ("I had walked") to show that the action happened before the time of reporting.

quick_notes.title: Pronoun Change (SON)
quick_notes.detail: 1st Person (I/We) -> Subject. 2nd Person (You) -> Object. 3rd Person (He/She) -> No Change.
quick_notes.explanation: When we change direct speech into reported speech, the pronouns in the quoted sentence often need to change. The rule called SON helps you remember how: S stands for Subject, meaning first-person pronouns like I and We change to match the subject of the reporting verb. O stands for Object, meaning second-person pronoun You changes to match the object of the reporting verb. N stands for No Change, meaning third-person pronouns like He, She, It, and They stay exactly the same. For example, if Ravi says "I am happy," in reported speech it becomes "Ravi said that he was happy" because I changes to he (the subject). If you say "You are late," and you are speaking to Mohan, it becomes "I told Mohan that he was late" because You changes to he (the object). If Ravi says "She is here," it becomes "Ravi said that she was here" because She stays unchanged.

quick_notes.title: Time & Place words
quick_notes.detail: Today -> That day. Tomorrow -> The next day. Yesterday -> The previous day. Now -> Then. Here -> There.
quick_notes.explanation: When you tell someone what another person said, you often change time and place words to make the reported statement accurate from your new perspective. For example, if the original statement used the word "today," you change it to "that day" because "today" from the past is now a different day. Similarly, "tomorrow" becomes "the next day," "yesterday" becomes "the previous day," "now" becomes "then," and "here" becomes "there." These changes help your listener understand that you are talking about a past moment, not the present moment. Always think about the time and place from which the words are being reported, and adjust accordingly.

quick_notes.title: Interrogative
quick_notes.detail: Use "if/whether" for Yes/No questions. No "that" used with Wh-questions. (e.g., He said, "Where are you going?" -> He asked where I was going).
quick_notes.explanation: Interrogative sentences ask a question. When you change a direct question into an indirect or reported speech question, you must follow two main rules. For yes/no questions, which can be answered with yes or no, you join the reported part using "if" or "whether", and remove the question mark; for example, the direct question "Are you coming?" becomes "He asked if I was coming." For wh-questions, which start with words like what, where, when, who, or how, you must not use the word "that" after the reporting verb; instead, you simply keep the wh-word itself, like changing the direct question "Where are you going?" into "He asked where I was going." In both cases, change the verb tense and pronouns as in normal reported speech, and do not use a question mark at the end of the reported sentence.
